article.overview: A surface drilling robot is a robotic system that penetrates lunar regolith or harder ground to collect or analyse material from below the surface. The payload class is defined by its function rather than by one design. Flown or operated examples to date include the Soviet Luna 24 automated drill (1976), the Chang'e-5 robotic core drill (2020) and NASA's TRIDENT drill, which was carried to the Moon on Intuitive Machines' IM-2 mission (Athena lander) in March 2025. Several other drills, including the ESA ProSEED system and drilling concepts for Mars, are in development or proposed and have not flown.
article.description: A surface drilling robot combines a drill head, a drive mechanism, a depth-control system and, in many designs, a sample-handling route that moves cuttings or cores to an instrument. The robot can be operated from Earth through commands, which distinguishes it from the crewed Apollo drill. NASA states that TRIDENT was designed to stop at any depth as commanded from the ground and that it deposits samples on the surface for analysis by the MSOLO mass spectrometer. NASA describes the drill as lightweight and low-power and as 1 meter long; no maximum depth, bite size, mass or power figure is given in that NASA article. Drilling into the Moon is difficult because the upper layers are a loose, dusty regolith that may contain rocks and, near the poles, icy material. A drill must cut through several materials, keep its samples uncontaminated and report what it finds.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar surface drill is to obtain subsurface material for analysis. Stratigraphy and regolith history: core samples preserve layering and the way the regolith has been built up by impacts; Chang'e-5 drill analysis reports layer boundaries at roughly 28.7 cm and 70 cm. Volatile prospecting: cold-trapped water ice and other volatiles may exist in permanently shadowed polar regions. ESA's PROSPECT description gives expected temperatures of typically -150 degrees C beneath the surface and lower than -200 degrees C in some areas, which is why volatiles could be preserved in the samples. Whether such deposits exist in usable quantities is a research question, not a measured result. In-situ resource assessment: TRIDENT was flown in part to assess whether drilled material could support future resource use; this is a mission objective rather than a demonstrated result. Geotechnical measurement: TRIDENT is described as measuring the strength, compactness and temperature of the regolith; these are mission goals and their published results were not verified for this article.
article.operating_principle: Most surface drills described here are rotary-percussive. The drill head spins to cut into the ground and hammers to break hard material into fragments. Cuttings move up the flutes of an auger. In the TRIDENT design, as described in secondary summaries of the mission, the drill advances in short bites of about 10 cm, retracts, and deposits the cuttings on the surface, where instruments can analyse them. A depth sensor or commanded stop limits penetration. The Chang'e-5 drill was a hollow core drill. A telemetry and imaging study of that drill reports a dip angle of about 2.3 degrees and a depth error under 2 mm. A separate analysis reports that regolith particles obstructed the sampling entry of the hollow tool at about 1 m, and a sealing device was developed in response. The Luna 24 drill is described in one secondary source as a rotary-percussion LB-09 that changed mode beyond 120 cm; this mode detail was not confirmed against a primary archive.
article.scientific_importance: Drilled samples allow scientists to study material that surface photography and remote sensing cannot reach. Core samples from the Apollo 15 and Luna 24 missions, and from Chang'e-5, have supported lunar science, and surface drilling is a way to obtain a depth-resolved core without a crewed mission. For volatile studies, drilled samples enable heating and chemical analysis of material that was never exposed to the warmer surface. The scientific value of a drill depends on how well the depth of each sample is known. Chang'e-5 analyses show that most recovered material came from the upper layers and that the drill met rocky ground below about 73.8 cm, which limits what the core can reveal about deeper layers.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a surface drilling robot. Drills differ in architecture (auger, hollow core, percussive or rotary-percussive), power source, depth capability and sample-handling route, so the values below describe specific instruments rather than the class. Where a value is not supported by a fetched source, it is shown as not publicly specified or as an unverified report.

examples.name: NASA TRIDENT (The Regolith and Ice Drill for Exploring New Terrain)
examples.type: Flown robotic lunar drill (carried by PRIME-1 on Intuitive Machines IM-2, Athena lander, landed 6 March 2025)
examples.mass_note: Not publicly confirmed. One NASA-hosted search-surfaced source reports 16 kg; a secondary source gives a limit of under 20 kg. Not verified from a fetched primary document; not used as structured data.
examples.depth_capability: Commanded from the ground; no maximum depth stated in the fetched NASA article. Secondary sources describe a 1 m design depth.
examples.sample_bite_note: Described in secondary sources as about 10 cm long per bite; not confirmed against a NASA primary source.
examples.power_note: Described by NASA as low-power. A search-surfaced NASA-hosted source reports 200 W for each of the rotary and percussive actuators; not verified against a fetched document.
examples.drilling_outcome: NASA reports the drill was deployed and its actuators performed as designed through multiple movement stages, including full extension and percussive hammering. Secondary reports state the lander's orientation prevented the drill from penetrating the surface and collecting a soil sample. No fetched source confirms a completed soil sample; the drilling result is unresolved.
examples.qualification: Flown on IM-2 (March 2025); operations were far shorter than the planned 10 days according to NASA.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: There is no single dimension set for a surface drilling robot. TRIDENT is described by NASA as 1 meter long; its diameter is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The Chang'e-5 drill is described as a 2-m class robotic drill. Dimensions must be set by the intended depth, the sample-handling route and the lander or rover accommodation, and they should not be compared across unlike designs.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass values are not confirmed for any drill described here. TRIDENT mass is reported as 16 kg in one NASA-hosted search-surfaced source and as under 20 kg in a secondary source; neither was verified from a fetched primary document. Mass affects launch requirements, lander capacity and deployment design, so these values must be confirmed before any compatibility assessment.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: TRIDENT is described as low-power; one search-surfaced NASA-hosted source reports 200 W for each of its rotary and percussive actuators, which was not verified. The Mars deep drill concept has a 100 W power budget (JPL). Other drills' power figures are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A surface drill must operate in extreme thermal conditions. Surface temperatures vary widely between lunar day and night, and ESA's PROSPECT description gives subsurface temperatures near -150 degrees C and below -200 degrees C in some polar areas. The drill and its electronics need thermal protection and a way of keeping mechanisms within their operating range. The drill also needs a stable mounting. Its reaction forces must be taken by the lander or rover, and the platform must be level and secure. The Athena landing shows how strongly the platform affects the drill: a lander lying on its side can prevent deployment and sampling. Power and data connections, dust protection and a reliable command loop from Earth are also needed, given the communication delays and the lunar night. Ground material is another variable. Regolith, rock, basalt and icy mixtures behave differently under drilling, and the Chang'e-5 analyses show that rocky ground and particle obstruction can end a core early.
article.limitations: Depth reached is not the same as depth sampled: Chang'e-5 analyses show most material came from the upper 73.8 cm. Hollow-core drills can be obstructed by regolith particles at the sampling entry. A surface drill gives samples from a single location and cannot establish lateral variation without repeated drilling. The drilling capability of a robotic system depends on the lander's orientation and stability, which the TRIDENT flight illustrates. Several figures in this article come from secondary summaries or index pages and are flagged as such.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface drilling robot is integrated onto a lander or rover payload and delivered to the surface as part of a larger lunar mission. The TRIDENT drill was part of the PRIME-1 payload carried by Intuitive Machines' IM-2 mission.
transportation_process: Earth integration: the drill is integrated onto a lander or rover payload compartment, with mounting points, thermal insulation and electrical interfaces defined by the host spacecraft. For TRIDENT, the drill was part of PRIME-1 on IM-2.
Launch and lunar transfer: the payload is launched on a launch vehicle and transferred to the Moon. IM-2 launched from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on 26 February 2025 (NASA).

Landing and delivery: the lander delivers the payload to the surface. IM-2 touched down about 400 m from its intended site, Mons Mouton, near the lunar south pole, on 6 March 2025 (NASA). The lander came to rest on its side in a crater.

Deployment and setup: NASA reports the drill was deployed on the surface and its actuators performed as designed. Subsequent drilling depends on the lander's orientation, which secondary reports say prevented soil penetration on this mission.

Power, data and thermal interfaces: NASA reports about 6.6 gigabytes of data returned from IM-2, with PRIME-1 contributing some of it. The power source, data route and thermal interface of the drill were not verified in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The TRIDENT drill was deployed from the IM-2 lander as part of PRIME-1, as reported by NASA. Other drills' deployment methods are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Deployment design depends on whether the drill is mounted on a lander, a rover or a dedicated deployment mechanism.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15 astronauts used a drill for deep core sampling in 1971. Luna 24 used an automated drill to return about 170 g of lunar material in 1976. Chang'e-5 used a robotic drill to collect samples in 2020. TRIDENT was carried by IM-2 in 2025.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The TRIDENT-IM-2 flight is documented. Compatibility of any drill with another lander or rover is not verified in this article and must be assessed against verified interface specifications (mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, power, data and thermal interfaces). No compatibility claim is made for any other spacecraft.

article.historical_significance: Surface drilling has a long history in lunar science. The Apollo 15 crew used a rotary-percussive drill to take a deep core in 1971, and the Soviet Luna 24 spacecraft used an automated drill to return about 170 g of lunar material in 1976. Chang'e-5 returned robotic drill samples in 2020. The TRIDENT drill, carried to the Moon in 2025, is a NASA attempt to add a robotic drill with an in-situ mass spectrometer, and its outcome is an important part of the evidence for future robotic drilling. None of these examples is described as a first in every respect, because the sources reviewed did not establish that claim.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: TRIDENT drilling outcome: NASA reports successful deployment and actuator performance; secondary reports state the drill did not penetrate. No fetched source confirms a soil sample. TRIDENT mass and power: sources disagree and were not verified from fetched primary documents. TRIDENT diameter and bite size: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Chang'e-5 and Luna 24 figures: values are from index pages, abstracts or secondary summaries; full texts and NSSDC catalogue entries were not retrieved. Luna 24 depth: sources report 225 cm, about 2.5 m and about 2 m. ESA ProSEED status and depth: the ESA page reviewed is out of date and describes a Luna-27 flight plan; a secondary summary describes redirection to a NASA CLPS mission. Apollo 15 core figures: 242 cm and 236 cm come from a secondary summary of Carrier (1974) and a compendium draft; the primary mission report was not fetched. Environmental performance of any future drill in polar conditions is not demonstrated by any source reviewed here beyond the reported observations.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue ID 278, name 'Surface drilling robot' and category 14 'Robotics, mobility and deployment technology' confirmed against lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.

TRIDENT drilling outcome is unresolved: NASA (April 2025 article) reports successful deployment and actuator performance; secondary reports state the drill could not penetrate the surface because of lander orientation. No fetched source confirms a soil sample.

TRIDENT mass (16 kg in one NASA-hosted search-surfaced source; under 20 kg in a secondary source), power (200 W per actuator in one search-surfaced source), and bite size (about 10 cm in secondary sources) are unverified. TRIDENT diameter is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Structured mass_kg and power_w left null.
The TRIDENT design review PDFs (NTRS SRR2024 and LPSC 2024 papers) and the Zacny 2025 paper could not be text-extracted by the fetch tool; their specifications were not used.

Chang'e-5 figures (1 m depth, 259.72 g, 73.8 cm, layers at 28.7 cm and 70 cm, 2.3 degree dip, under 2 mm depth error) come from index pages and abstracts; full texts were not retrieved. The Chang'e-5 2020 sample return date is general knowledge not checked against a fetched source.

Luna 24 depth conflicts across sources (225 cm, about 250 cm, 2.5 m); the 225 cm figure is from russianspaceweb and is not confirmed against an NSSDC or primary archive. The NSSDC master catalogue entry (COSPAR 1976-081) was identified but not retrieved.

ESA ProSEED: the ESA page reviewed was last updated 1 September 2019 and describes a Luna-27 flight plan; a secondary summary says the programme is being redirected to a NASA CLPS mission. Drill depth is not stated on the ESA page; the 1 m depth in a secondary search summary is unverified. Leonardo and Open University roles are from a secondary summary.

Apollo 15 deep core figures (242 cm recovered length; 236 +/- 1 cm stem penetration) come from a secondary search summary of Carrier (1974) and a Meyer compendium draft; the primary Apollo 15 mission report was not fetched. The Apollo drill is crewed and included as a historical reference only.

The NASA Apollo-to-Artemis drilling feature was fetched for TRIDENT and Apollo 15 context and image URLs. A separate NASA Lunar Surface Journal drilling page did not contain drill specifications when fetched and was not used.
The Mars deep drill example is a proposed non-lunar concept from the JPL subsurface-access page; it is not a lunar payload and its values are not lunar specifications.
Image visual content was not inspected; captions and credits are taken from the source pages named in each image object. Image rights and reuse caveats apply; no public-domain status is asserted.
Lunar landing-site or location recommendations are deferred by user and are not included.
